Abstract
Thermo-mechanical compliant devices are commonly designed with small-strain linear elas-
ticity and temperature-independent material properties, even though they might operate hun-
dreds of kelvin above ambient where both assumptions are questionable. In this work, we
quantify the efect and cost of each assumption in multi-material topology optimization of ther
mally actuated compliant devices. To this end, we introduce a physics-informed, simultaneous
analysis-and-design framework with (i) a finite-strain quadratic-Hencky (logarithmic-strain) con-
stitutive model whose isotropic thermal eigenstrain admits an exact additive split in log-strain
space, and (ii) temperature-dependent conductivity, thermal expansion, and elastic moduli for a
titanium–copper–steel material system. We optimize a thermal actuator and a thermal gripper
at three design temperatures under both a baseline model and the full physics, subject to mass
and manufacturability constraints. Every converged design is re-evaluated by verified nonlinear
finite element solvers in the full factorial of constitutive law and property model. The compar-
ison between the two factors reveals that the constitutive law is the decisive modeling choice:
These devices work as linkages where linear kinematics mistakes rotation for compressive strain;
its error therefore grows with the design temperature and concentrates on the very layouts that
exploit rotation best. Because a linear optimizer also steers away from the rotation-rich mecha-
nisms that would expose this bias, the model can deceptively appear trustworthy when validated
against its own designs. Designing with the full physics yields consistently stronger and more
temperature-robust devices at a modest increase in design-time cost.<sup>1</sup>

1 Introduction
Topology optimization (TO) is an established computational design method that finds the optimal spatial
distribution of material in a design domain directly from the governing physics and design requirements. TO
has matured into a standard tool for designing compliant mechanisms, thermal devices, and multi-physics
systems [1–5]. In thermo-mechanical TO, actuation is generated by constrained thermal expansion rather
than external loads, a principle widely exploited in micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) where elec-
trothermal actuators and grippers convert Joule heating or a prescribed thermal environment into controlled
strokes [6–9]. The design space is considerably richer in multi-material settings, where the optimizer arranges
several candidate metals to exploit their unique material properties subject to mass and manufacturability
constraints [10, 11].

Nearly all of this literature, including our own prior work [11], rests on two modeling conveniences. First,
the mechanical response is described by small-strain linear elasticity, even though the slender members and
distributed hinges that make a compliant mechanism efective undergo moderate rotations well before strains
become large [12–14]. Second, material properties are held constant. In the thermal-actuator literature the
constant values are often nondimensionalized and independent of the operating temperature [6–8,15]. Inves-
tigations that do use physical properties, adopt room temperature values despite the mismatch with operating
temperatures [16,17]. Deng and Suresh [18], for example, state that their reference room temperature serves
“only” to select material properties, and then optimize a titanium-alloy wing rib at ∆T = 270 K; our own
prior work [11] likewise uses room-temperature moduli and conductivities at a 673 K boundary temperature.
The convention is particularly damaging: at 673 K, copper (the dominant phase in the optimized devices of
this work) has an elastic modulus 15% below its room-temperature value and a mean coeficient of thermal
expansion 9% above it, while across the candidate metals the moduli drop by 15–21% and the thermal
conductivity of steel falls by 26% [19–22]. A room-temperature-anchored model misrepresents not only the
stifness of the device but also the thermal load that drives it.
Although restricted to linear elasticity, a small body of work does use temperature-dependent proper-
ties and reports concrete gains. Tang et al. [23] make conductivity, elastic tensor, and expansion coefi-
cient temperature-dependent under large gradients, carrying the dependence through the adjoint, and find
constant-property optimization significantly inaccurate; Zheng et al. [24] reach the same conclusion over 293–
773 K. For multi-material design, Chen et al. [25] report that the temperature-dependent modulus dominates
compliance while the expansion coeficient principally reshapes the material distribution compared against
room-temperature-anchored baselines. A better constant-property practice evaluates the properties at the
design temperature; we therefore adopt this stronger convention as the baseline of this study and quantify
the potential benefit of incorporating fully temperature-dependent properties. Both modeling conveniences
bias the very objective that the optimizer maximizes, i.e., the predicted output stroke. Since the optimizer
is free to exploit any inaccuracy of its physics model, such biases do not merely misreport performance; they
can also steer the search toward designs whose advantage is an artifact of the model. Quantifying these
efects, separately and jointly, is the main goal of this paper.
Geometrically nonlinear TO of compliant mechanisms has an established history built on Green–Lagrange
kinematics with St. Venant–Kirchhof or neo-Hookean energies [12–14], together with interpolation schemes
that stabilize low-density regions at finite strain [26]. Extensions to thermally driven finite-strain problems
are comparatively recent: Chung et al. [27] combined level-set TO with nonlinear thermoelasticity, Sui
et al. [28] designed thermo-hyperelastic structures via inverse-motion form finding, and Granlund et al.
[29] optimized compliant mechanisms under transient thermal loading with a multi-material neo-Hookean
model. Temperature-dependent properties have likewise received attention in thermo-elastic TO under large
temperature gradients [23]. The Hencky (logarithmic) strain measure, however, has essentially not been
used in thermo-mechanical TO; its appearances in TO are limited to purely mechanical settings such as
hyperelastic ground structures [30] and material-point-method TO of large-deformation mechanisms [31].
This measure is particularly well suited to thermo-mechanical design: for isotropic thermal expansion, the
logarithmic thermal eigenstrain acts as an exact additive and isotropic ofset to the elastic strain across

with respect to thermal stretch. The quadratic-Hencky energy is furthermore an excellent model of real
metals up to moderate elastic strains [32–34], precisely the regime of metallic compliant devices.

The results reveal a sharp asymmetry between the two assumptions. These devices function as linkages

compressive strain comparable to the thermal eigenstrain that drives the device: its error grows from 2–3% of
stroke at 673 K to 8–11% at 1073 K. For the layouts that rely most heavily on rotation, this error consumes
up to a third of the stroke and inverts the ranking of the best designs at high temperatures. In contrast,
the constant-property model that is anchored at the design temperature alters the results by less than one

a less physically relevant temperature, or if the devices were subjected to temperature gradients significantly

the best designs by far more, design tools should be audited by independent higher-fidelity re-evaluation
rather than by self-assessment.
The extensions we consider most pressing address the physics this study deliberately held fixed. First,
material nonlinearity: at high homologous temperatures (copper at 1073 K operates near 0.8 of its melting
point) metals yield, creep and relax, and the quadratic-Hencky energy is precisely the elastic core of mul-
tiplicative finite-strain inelasticity so the framework extends naturally to plasticity- and creep-aware design
where we should consider stress and stability constraints. Second, transient response: replacing steady con-

bandwidth and cyclic behavior rather than a single hot state. This is particularly important for capturing
the regime in which creep and thermal ratcheting accumulate over repeated strokes. Finally, optimizing
over a range of operating temperatures, rather than at a single design point, would maximize expected or
worst-case performance across an operating window and yield devices that tolerate uncertain and drifting
thermal environments by construction. The transferability results of this study, where moderately hot train-

steps would elevate the framework from a controlled model trial to robust design of dynamically actuated
devices in service.

framework the upgrade replaces one energy density in the training loss rather than a solver; it costs a factor of
about 1.4 in design time, returns 4–12% more best-design stroke and produces the most temperature-robust
devices with moderate-temperature designs transferring best along the nearly afine stroke–temperature re-
sponse. Lastly, since a linear model misjudges its own designs by only about one percent while misjudging
the best designs by far more, design tools should be audited by independent higher-fidelity re-evaluation
rather than by self-assessment.
The extensions we consider most pressing address the physics this study deliberately held fixed. First,
material nonlinearity: at high homologous temperatures (copper at 1073 K operates near 0.8 of its melting
point) metals yield, creep and relax, and the quadratic-Hencky energy is precisely the elastic core of mul-
tiplicative finite-strain inelasticity so the framework extends naturally to plasticity- and creep-aware design
where we should consider stress and stability constraints. Second, transient response: replacing steady con-
duction with transient thermal loading and Joule-heating coupling would let the optimizer shape actuation
bandwidth and cyclic behavior rather than a single hot state. This is particularly important for capturing
the regime in which creep and thermal ratcheting accumulate over repeated strokes. Finally, optimizing
over a range of operating temperatures, rather than at a single design point, would maximize expected or
worst-case performance across an operating window and yield devices that tolerate uncertain and drifting
thermal environments by construction. The transferability results of this study, where moderately hot train-
ing temperatures already produce the strongest all-around designs are an encouraging starting point. These
steps would elevate the framework from a controlled model trial to robust design of dynamically actuated
devices in service.
